item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 5 Nov: Nasdaq 100 plunges 6.36% as AI selloff spreads
item.description:
• Nasdaq 100 suffers worst day since 2020
  • Magnificent 7: What are the technicals telling traders for each of those companies him
  • WTI crude oil settles at $90.52, up 2.72% as buyers defend key support
  • Non-farm payrolls preview: October numbers show a skew
  • Europe Close: AI and chip liquidation drags equities lower in US, but Europe is mixed.
  • Bitcoin falls with risk off sentiment. The price is testing a key swing area target.
  • The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout
  • Crude oil tests the key confluence area and finds willing buyers
  • Fed's Barkin: Gradual pace of hikes "makes sense"
  • Marco Rubio ‘on resignation watch’ - report
  • Fed's Hammack: Gradual rate hikes are the best way to get inflation to target
  • US Q3 productivity +3.6% vs +2.8% expected
  • US initial jobless claims 189K vs 196K estimate
  • Morning Kickstart: BOE hikes to 4% as sterling struggles to hold its gains
  • investingLive European news wrap: BoE raises bank rate to 4.00% as expected
  • BoE Governor Bailey says there is a case for another 25bps hike if war doesn't end

Wednesday’s rotation out of AI and into the broader market turned into a broad selloff on Thursday. The Nasdaq 100 took the biggest hit, but the Russell 2000 fell 4.45% and the Dow lost more than it gained the day before. Falling Treasury yields helped gold catch a bid. They did little for tech stocks or Bitcoin.

Crude went the other way. After Wednesday’s plunge on hopes for an end to the Iran war, reports of fresh Gulf shipping incidents put the risk to supplies back in focus. The dollar was mixed, with the Australian dollar taking the biggest hit among the majors and the yen holding up best.

The dollar gains against the Aussie but loses ground to the yen

The USD was strongest against the AUD, with AUDUSD down 1.13% to 0.6925. It was weakest against the JPY, with USDJPY down 0.49% to 157.64. Lower U.S. yields were consistent with the move in USDJPY, while the Aussie fell alongside other risk-sensitive assets.

Elsewhere, EURUSD fell 0.09% to 1.1217, GBPUSD fell 0.17% to 1.3448, and NZDUSD fell 0.50% to 0.5592. USDCAD rose 0.31% to 1.4020 despite the rebound in crude, while USDCHF edged down 0.02% to 0.8166.

Treasury yields fall, led by the 2-year

  • 2-year yield 4.4665%, down 11.45 basis points

  • 5-year yield 4.6098%, down 7.82 basis points

  • 10-year yield 4.8408%, down 5.12 basis points

  • 30-year yield 5.2581%, down 2.19 basis points

The curve steepened as short-term yields fell more than long-term yields. The size of the move at the front end stood out given that jobless claims came in below expectations and crude bounced.

U.S. stocks close sharply lower

  • Dow industrial average −1,833.16 points (−3.44%) to 51,528.16

  • S&P 500 −334.77 points (−4.35%) to 7,353.85

  • Nasdaq Composite −1,421.52 points (−5.52%) to 24,315.00

  • Russell 2000 −127.11 points (−4.45%) to 2,729.84

  • Nasdaq 100 −1,807.36 points (−6.36%) to 26,629.81

AI suppliers lead the selloff

The selling hit memory, storage, chip equipment and data-center suppliers. Micron was down about 12% during the session as investors questioned how quickly the AI buildout would translate into orders for suppliers. That matters across the supply chain, from the memory that goes into AI accelerators to the drives that store the data.

All seven Magnificent 7 stocks were lower in my late-session check. Nvidia and Tesla were the only two underperforming both Nasdaq indices at that point. Apple and Alphabet held up best, down 1.27% and 1.53%, respectively. Magnificent 7 coverage

Europe closes mixed

  • Spain’s IBEX 35 +0.59%

  • France’s CAC 40 +0.34%

  • Germany’s DAX −0.43%

  • U.K.’s FTSE 100 −0.43%

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB −1.03%

InvestingLive’s European close

U.S. data hold up as markets look to Washington

Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 versus 196,000 expected, while third-quarter productivity rose 3.6% versus 2.8% expected. In the U.K., the Bank of England raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 4.00%, citing inflation pressure tied to the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices. Sterling still slipped against the dollar.

After the European close, Adam Button highlighted two questions coming out of the midterms. Will the Trump administration change course on Iran, and will it move to ease tariffs as Congress presses for changes? The answers matter for oil supply risk and for the inflation outlook. InvestingLive’s Washington coverage

Crude rebounds as Gulf shipping risks resurface

WTI futures settled at $90.52 a barrel, up $2.40 or 2.72%, and were quoted later at $91.06, up 3.34%. Wednesday’s drop of more than 8% reflected hopes for a path out of the Iran war. On Thursday, reports of several shipping incidents in the Gulf reminded traders that the risk to supply is still there. Treasury yields fell even as crude recovered. WTI settlement and Gulf shipping coverage

Gold gains while silver and copper fall

Spot gold rose 0.68% to $4,088.02. Lower Treasury yields reduced the opportunity cost of holding gold, and the equity selloff was consistent with some demand for a haven. Silver fell 0.94% to $51.76 and copper dropped 3.51% to $6.2035. The weakness in those two was consistent with their greater exposure to industrial demand.

Bitcoin gives back its rebound

Bitcoin was down 5.69% at $75,861 late in the session. It rallied alongside stocks on Wednesday and fell alongside them on Thursday, trading much more like the Nasdaq than gold. See technical post here.

What carries into Friday

The first question is whether buyers return to the chip and data-center names that led the market lower. I’ll also be watching whether the 2-year yield holds onto its decline and whether crude keeps its rebound. If Gulf shipping risks keep oil bid while short-term yields stay under pressure, that will be a divergence worth following.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq 100 suffers worst day since 2020
item.description:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% on Thursday, its worst day since 2020, as investors sold everything from memory and storage stocks to chip equipment makers and data-center suppliers. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%, the S&P 500 dropped 4.35%, and the Dow lost 1,833 points. All three had their worst day since April 2025.

A day after the Dow surged nearly 1,600 points, it gave back the entire gain and then some. The Russell 2000 fell 4.45%, and all 30 Dow stocks closed lower. The selling was most intense in the AI trade, but by the close it had spread well beyond it.

Investors continued to weigh what the midterm results could mean for the pace of the AI data-center buildout. Treasury yields moved lower and gold caught a bid as stocks sold off. Lower yields can help growth stocks, but today they came alongside a broad move away from risk and offered little relief to tech.

U.S. stock market closing levels

  • Dow Jones Industrial Average −1,833.16 points (−3.44%) to 51,528.16

  • S&P 500 −334.77 points (−4.35%) to 7,353.85

  • Nasdaq Composite −1,421.52 points (−5.52%) to 24,315.00

  • Russell 2000 −127.11 points (−4.45%) to 2,729.84

  • Nasdaq 100 −1,807.36 points (−6.36%) to 26,629.81

Every Dow stock fell

Nvidia led the Dow lower with a 9.26% decline. Cisco fell 7.62%, Goldman Sachs lost 6.44%, Caterpillar dropped 6.39%, and Honeywell fell 5.55%. Verizon (−0.04%) and Coca-Cola (−0.07%) came closest to finishing flat.

The breadth numbers tell the same story. S&P 500 decliners outnumbered advancers 411 to 75. Across the Nasdaq, 2,822 stocks fell and 463 rose, a little more than six decliners for every advancer. On the NYSE Composite, the count was 1,512 down and 288 up.

The AI and chip names that fell 10% or more

The closing watchlist showed 22 individual stocks down at least 10%, plus the VanEck Semiconductor ETF. Sandisk led the declines, and the losses ran through nearly every part of the chip and data-center supply chain.

  • Memory and storage — Sandisk −22.26%, Micron Technology −17.46%, Western Digital −17.35%.

  • Chip designers and manufacturers — AMD −17.26%, Arm Holdings −13.08%, Taiwan Semiconductor −10.78%, Texas Instruments −10.70%, Broadcom −10.43%, Intel −10.33%, Monolithic Power Systems −10.28%.

  • Networking, connectivity and optics — Astera Labs −19.62%, Lumentum −18.68%, Credo Technology −17.71%, Marvell Technology −16.43%, Coherent −12.98%, Arista Networks −10.82%.

  • Semiconductor equipment and components — Lam Research −16.36%, Applied Materials −13.58%, SkyWater Technology −13.40%, KLA −13.35%.

  • Data-center compute and power — Nebius Group −14.95%, Bloom Energy −16.41%.

  • Semiconductor ETF — VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) −11.21%.

All seven Mag 7 stocks fall, led by Tesla and Nvidia

There was no green in the Magnificent Seven, but there was a big difference in how the stocks held up. Tesla fell 10.77% and Nvidia lost 9.26%. They were the only two to fall more than the S&P 500 (−4.35%), the Nasdaq Composite (−5.52%) and the Nasdaq 100 (−6.36%).

Apple held up best, down 1.53%, followed by Amazon (−2.19%) and Alphabet (−2.20%). Microsoft and Meta also held up better than the three broader indices, although both fell more than the Dow (−3.44%).

  • Tesla −10.77% to $343.69

  • Nvidia −9.26% to $181.60

  • Meta Platforms −3.96% to $605.08

  • Microsoft −3.58% to $535.93

  • Alphabet −2.20% to $282.57

  • Amazon −2.19% to $260.21

  • Apple −1.53% to $344.17

On the next bounce, I’ll be watching Tesla and Nvidia. If buyers step in and those two can hold their gains, it would be an early sign that the selling pressure is easing in the hardest-hit megacaps.

The YTD scorecard after the selloff

The YTD numbers put the selloff in perspective. SanDisk fell more than 20% on the day and was still up more than 200% for the year. Micron and AMD each fell about 17%, yet both held on to substantial YTD gains. Nvidia and Broadcom were already on the other side of the ledger by the end of the session. The selling hit the chip stocks hard, but the cushion going into the day varied considerably.

The Magnificent 7 are split three up and four down. Apple leads the group at roughly +27% YTD, with Amazon and Microsoft still up double digits. Tesla is the weakest at about −24%. Outside tech, Target, Chevron, ExxonMobil and Coca-Cola are still sitting on sizable gains. Meanwhile, some of the deepest losses on the watchlist are in software, with Intuit down about 46% and Oracle off 41%.

All five major U.S. indices are still positive for 2026 after the November 5 selloff. The Russell 2000 is the only one still up double digits, while the Nasdaq Composite has the smallest gain. AP News

Price returns through the November 5 close, measured from the December 31, 2025 close.

The Nasdaq Composite went into the session up about 10.7% for the year and came out up just 4.6%. The S&P 500’s gain narrowed from about 12.3% to 7.4%.

What traders should watch after a selloff like this

Sellers have control heading into the next session. The first thing I’ll watch on a bounce is whether it can hold and whether more stocks participate. A few megacaps can lift an index early even while most stocks are still falling. If breadth improves and the chip stocks that led the decline start to hold their rebounds, buyers have more evidence that the selling is easing. If those stocks give back their gains and breadth stays weak, the burden remains on the buyers.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Magnificent 7: What are the technicals telling traders for each of those companies him
item.description:
In the video above, I take a look at the Magnificent 7 as the broader U.S. indices sell off sharply. The S&P 500 is down around 4%, the Nasdaq Composite is down 5.10%, and the Nasdaq 100 is down 5.75%. All seven stocks are lower, but only two are falling more than all three indices. Those two are Nvidia and Tesla.

Apple and Alphabet hold up best

Apple leads the group with a decline of 1.27%, followed by Alphabet, down 1.53%. Amazon is down 2.49%, Microsoft is lower by 3.64%, and Meta is down 3.87%. All five are outperforming both Nasdaq indices, although Apple and Alphabet are doing so by a much wider margin than Microsoft and Meta.

For Apple and Alphabet, the question is whether that relative strength shows up at support. Can buyers lean against a level and put in a low? If they can, the next test is whether the price can get back above the first resistance level and stay there. That would give buyers something to build on.

Nvidia and Tesla see the most selling

Nvidia is down 8.55%, while Tesla is the weakest of the seven with a decline of 11.19%. Both are falling considerably more than the Nasdaq 100. For those two, I’m watching what happens on a bounce. If sellers lean against a broken support level on the way back up, that old floor becomes a ceiling and keeps the downside bias intact. If the price gets back above that level and holds, sellers have lost some of their control.

The levels that matter from here

On a day like this, the size of the decline tells you where the pressure is. The technical levels give you a way to judge whether that pressure is easing or building. Does the price break support and stay below it, opening the door to the next downside target? Or does it dip below, snap back above, and force sellers to rethink the break?

That distinction also helps define risk. If buyers lean against support, they have a nearby level that tells them when the trade is going against them. If sellers lean against resistance on a bounce, they have the same kind of barometer on the topside.

Watch the video above for the key levels in all seven stocks, where buyers or sellers can lean, and what would shift the bias from here.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: WTI crude oil settles at $90.52, up 2.72% as buyers defend key support
item.description:
U.S. crude oil futures settled at $90.52 a barrel on Thursday, up $2.40 or 2.72% from Wednesday’s $88.12 settlement. The rebound follows a drop of more than 8% on Wednesday, when the U.S. midterm results raised hopes that a Democratic-controlled Congress would increase pressure on the Trump administration to end the war with Iran.

Gulf shipping risk is back in focus

On Wednesday, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats would seek to end the war, pointing to Congress’s control over spending. By Thursday, traders were again weighing the risk to oil shipments. Reuters reported that at least five vessels had reported incidents in the Gulf since Sunday, citing UK Maritime Trade Operations. Iran’s foreign minister also spoke with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts about diplomatic efforts. The prospect of de-escalation helped take some risk premium out of oil on Wednesday. The shipping reports gave traders a reason to put some of it back in on Thursday.

Wednesday’s U.S. inventory report also showed draws in crude, gasoline and distillates for the week ended October 30. The draws offered some support heading into Thursday’s session.

Buyers defended $86.65–$86.93. Can they get above $91.56?

On the WTI chart, the selloff reached $86.65, right near the 200-day moving average at the time. The 100-day moving average was between that low and the 50% midpoint of the rally from the July low at $86.93. That gave buyers a well-defined area to lean against, and they did.

The next test is $91.56, the broken 38.2% retracement of that same rally. The futures settlement was $1.04 below it. Move above $91.56 and stay above, and buyers would have more room to retrace Wednesday’s selloff. Stall there and sellers have a level to lean against. A break back below $86.65–$86.93 would put the 61.8% retracement at $82.30 in play.

Trading takeaway

A bounce off support tells you where buyers were willing to step in. The next clue comes at former support. If buyers can reclaim $91.56 and hold it on a pullback, they’ll have a closer level to define their risk. If sellers defend it, the bounce remains vulnerable to a retest of the lows.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market is waiting for signals from Donald Trump
item.description:
I spoke to Reuters earlier today about the state of markets and my comments boiled down to this:

"There are two ​paths Trump can go down - he can double down on unpopular trade ​wars or he can listen to the electorate and change course," said Adam Button, chief currency analyst at investingLive.

That's the crossroads we are at right now and I think it shows some of the tension in markets.

An early sign we got was on replacing Pete Hegseth:

“No, I think he’s doing a very good job.”

Of course, Trump has said that many times before replacing staff, so I wouldn't take it as the final word. It's worth noting though that George H. W. Bush fired Donald Rumsfeld the day after the 2006 midterms, in large part due to the unpopular Iran war.

Trump did also tease at Hegseth taking the Tennessee Senate seat after its senator won the Governorship, soemthing he could in January.

Alternatively, House member Thomas Massie has pledge to start impeach Hegseth, and there's ample evidence that they could get the votes to do it, either before or after the new Congress is sworn in. Many Senators will be looking to reframe their anti-war, America First chops and Hegseth is a convenient scapegoat.

At the same time, there is a big distinction in how he's removed. If it's from Trump, it will be a sign that he's sick of the Iran war and will end it. If it's Congress, that still leaves a pro-war President in power.

In terms of the timeline, earlier NYT reporting about three aircraft carriers in the Gulf was incorrect. The USS Roosevelt will arrive in the Gulf in mid-November and that could be the window for strikes. There is talk the USS George Washington needs to depart the area soon so there is only a short overlap.

There is a similar dynamic unfolding around tariffs. Congress has lost patience with USMCA tariffs and perhaps some others. Expect some action on that either in the lame duck session or early next year.

Again, Trump has the option of cutting a deal beforehand and there's talk deals are close with Canada and Mexico. If he does that, it could bring down the temperature but Congress may still want to go further and repeal some tariffs to show they're fighting to bring down the cost of living.

One thing that worries me is that Trump reposted this message:

If he decides to double down on his worst instincts, it will keep inflation high, make the Fed's job harder and likely lead the market to price in even more Democrat gains in 2028.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Europe Close: AI and chip liquidation drags equities lower in US, but Europe is mixed.
item.description:
As London and European traders head home, the main story is the liquidation in US stocks. AI and chip names are taking the hardest hit as investors weigh the path forward after the US midterm elections. Yesterday, the Dow surged nearly 1,600 points even as parts of the AI trade struggled. Today, the Dow has given back most of that gain, the Russell 2000 is down more than 4%, and the Nasdaq 100 is down more than 5%. The selling has reached beyond the chipmakers into the power and infrastructure names tied to the AI buildout.

The Nasdaq indices have bounced off their lows, but the Dow and Russell are still right on theirs. For the S&P 500, the September low near 7,511 is the first level buyers need to get back above to take some pressure off. Stay below it, and the 200-day moving average near 7,323 and the swing area at 7,300–7,321 come into focus.

European stocks finish mixed as the BOE hikes

Spain’s IBEX 35 led the gains at +0.59%, followed by France’s CAC 40 at +0.34%. Germany’s DAX and the UK’s FTSE 100 each fell 0.43%, while Italy’s FTSE MIB was the weakest of the major indices, down 1.03%.

The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4.00%, as expected. The vote was 8–1 on the quarter-point move, with Catherine Mann preferring a 50-basis-point hike. Governor Andrew Bailey said there was a case for another quarter-point hike if the war continued. UK construction PMI went the other way, falling to 43.6 from 46.1 and missing the 46.4 forecast. GBPUSD reached 1.3506 before easing back to 1.3481.

Fed officials favor gradual hikes as Treasury yields fall

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said policy needs to become restrictive to get inflation back to 2% and favored smaller, more frequent rate increases. Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin described policy as roughly neutral and also favored a gradual pace of hikes. He said he sees little sign that inflation is coming down and noted that firms are still looking to pass on higher costs.

On the data front, initial jobless claims fell to 189K versus 196K expected and a revised 195K previously. Continuing claims rose to 1.718 million from a revised 1.695 million. Third-quarter nonfarm productivity rose at a 3.6% annualized pace, while unit labor costs fell 0.7%. The next test comes Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET with the October employment report.

Treasury yields moved lower across the curve, with the biggest declines at the short end. The 2-year fell 9.2 basis points to 4.489%, the 5-year fell 7.8 basis points to 4.610%, the 10-year fell 5.7 basis points to 4.835%, and the 30-year fell 2.8 basis points to 5.252%. In Europe, Germany’s 10-year yield fell 3.1 basis points to 3.248%, while Italy’s rose 4.5 basis points to 4.364%. That widened the Italy–Germany spread by about 7.6 basis points.

The yen and gold catch a bid as Bitcoin slides

The dollar was mixed. USDJPY fell to 157.75, near its session low of 157.68, and USDCHF slipped to 0.8148. EURUSD edged up to 1.1236. The Australian dollar took the biggest hit among the majors shown, with AUDUSD down 0.76% at 0.6951, near its 0.6949 session low. NZDUSD fell to 0.5611, while USDCAD edged up to 1.3984.

Spot gold rose 1.20% to $4,109.17 as Treasury yields fell. Silver gained 0.29% to $52.40, while copper fell 2.29% to $6.2820. WTI crude rebounded 2.66% to $90.46. Bitcoin was down 5.56% at $75,960, trading more like the Nasdaq than gold in this session.

For the rest of the US session, I’ll be watching whether the Nasdaq bounce can get some help from the Dow and the Russell. Both are still leaning on their lows. A break below those lows would put the sellers back in position to extend the move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUDUSD sellers have pushed to the lowest level since mid-October. What next?
item.description:
Sellers have been leaning against retracement levels.

Going back to last week, the rally in the AUDUSD stalled near 0.7065, the 50% retracement of the move down from the September 9 high. Staying below, kept the seller in play. 

This week - on Monday - the pair set its high for the week as it tested the 100-hour and 100-day moving averages (blue lines on the chart below), both near 0.7030 at the time. The 38.2% retracement of the same move was just below at 0.7025.

The price moved below those levels and reached 0.6954 yesterday before snapping back higher as US stocks rallied and the market shifted back toward risk-on after the US elections. That bounce took the pair back toward 0.7025, where sellers leaned against the broken 38.2% retracement today.

The stock selloff took the AUDUSD to a fresh low.

As US stocks sold off today, so did the AUDUSD. The pair fell below the 200-hour moving average at 0.70159, the 100-hour moving average at 0.7003, and the swing area between 0.6989 and 0.6994. The selling picked up as the stock indices extended their declines. The pair broke yesterday’s 0.6954 low and traded down to 0.6949, its lowest level since October 19.

What now?

The close barometer for buyers and sellers is 0.6970–0.6977. That area represents the 38.2% to 50% retracement of the North American session’s trend move down from 0.7006 (see 5-minute chart) him. If buyers can’t get back above that zone, the path of least resistance remains to the downside, with the next support at 0.6932–0.6936. There are a number of prior swing lows and highs in that area, so watch how the price reacts on a test.

If buyers can get above 0.6977 and stay above it, the sellers lose some of their grip. That would put the broken 0.6989–0.6994 swing area back in play. Buyers would need to reclaim that area to build on a bounce, with the 100-hour moving average at 0.7003 the next hurdle.

Trading education. Match the retracement to the move you’re trading.

There are two different 38.2% retracements in this setup. The one at 0.7025 measures the broader move down from the September 9 high and helps explain where sellers showed up today. The one near 0.6970 measures the much shorter drop from 0.7006 and gives traders a closer level to judge the strength of the next bounce.

How much of the drop can buyers take back? If a bounce stalls near 0.6970, sellers are still keeping the correction shallow. If buyers get above the 50% midpoint near 0.6977 and hold it, they’ve taken back more than half of the session’s drop. That’s a reason for sellers to reassess their close risk. The next test is whether buyers can turn the former floor at 0.6989–0.6994 back into support.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil cracks are beginning to fall and refineries are pointing to more normalization
item.description:
The price of oil at $89 isn't that big of a problem for consumers or businesses. Crude has come down dramatically this week and a big part of that is expectations that Trump or Congress will find a way to open Hormuz and end the Iran war.

That remains to be seen but what hasn't changed is ultra-wide crack spreads. Normalized gasoline would be selling around $3.60-3.75 right now with diesel slightly higher with cracks around $22 (gasoline) and $30 (diesel). Because of all the refining tightness, gasoline has about a 60-cent premium and diesel at about +$2.25.

That's proven to be a big problem electorally and won't get better so long as the wars in Ukraine and Iran continue. If anything, they will worsen in time on potentially escalated strikes from Ukraine, Iran, the USA and Houthis.

From the looks of it, the prognosis is bad and winter sees higher distillate demand as well for heating. 

There is a positive sign though, the share prices of refineries are rolling over. Valero is a pure play and it's down 22% since October 13.

More broadly, the CRAK refiners ETF is down 16% from the October peak. 

In mid-October, the product tightness was extreme with $100 cracks. That's narrowed to $77 in jet fuel and even more in distillates. Diesel cracks are at $83 coimpared to $102 in mid-October and $92 on October 23. Notably, cracks haven't come in further in the past few days but refiners continue to fall. That could be a forward-looking indicator or market beta but it's worth watching. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin falls with risk off sentiment. The price is testing a key swing area target.
item.description:
Recall that Bitcoin moved higher with stocks on Wednesday, pushing back above $79,146 and into the old swing area that extends to $81,930. The move gave buyers a shot at taking back more control. To do that, they needed to get through the top of the area and stay above it. The rally stalled within the zone, and the price has since fallen back below $79,146.

Thursday. The risk-off crowd takes over

With the Nasdaq and chip stocks under pressure, Bitcoin has given back the rebound and moved back below its 100-day moving average at $76,950. The price was near $76,600 in the chart snapshot after testing the upper edge of the $74,925–$76,052 swing area. The 38.2% retracement of the summer rally comes in at $76,052, making that level the first downside barometer.

What next? The swing floor is the bigger test

For sellers, the 100-day MA at $76,950 is the close risk level. Stay below it, and the sellers keep the short-term advantage. Get below $76,052 and stay below, and the focus shifts to the swing-area floor at $74,925. A sustained break of that floor would open the door toward the 200-day MA at $73,195 and then the 50% retracement at $72,554.

For buyers, the first job is to hold the swing area and get back above $76,950. If they can get above that moving average and stay above it, the 100- and 200-hour MAs at $78,152 and $78,373 are the next targets. Above those, $79,146 comes back into focus.

In the video above, I talk about the technicals in more detail and explain the bias, the risks and targets.  

Education. How to lean against a swing area

A swing area gives traders a range where price has repeatedly changed direction. Here, $76,052 is the first level buyers can lean against, while $74,925 is the floor that defines the broader support area. If price breaks below $76,052 and quickly gets back above it, sellers who chased the break may have to cover. Getting above the 100 day MA would be a risk and bias defining confirmation level that if broken, would give buyers more confidence. If price stays below $76,052, the lower end of the range becomes the next test. That distinction lets traders define their risk before they enter and judge the trade by what price does at the level.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq Composite breaks the July low in 5.5% rout
item.description:
The rout is on in stock markets.

The Nasdaq Composite broke the 200-day moving average at the open and it's been non-stop selling from there. The index has now cut through the July low and is trading at the worst levels since April.

Nvidia is a major drag on the index and is now down 8.75% while Micron is getting destroyed, down 16.4%. I wrote about the reasons for the selloff in MU earlier. 

Meanwhile, shares of Apple are being seen as something of a safe haven as they've avoided the AI boom. They're down just 0.5% after hitting a 52-week high earlier. Berkshire Hathaway is also up 0.6% as its huge cash pile is seen as a possibility to deploy in a downturn. 

Yesterday we saw large gains in Microsoft and Amazon but those have faded to a large extent, with losses of 3.4% and 4.4%, respectively.

item.title: The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout
item.description:
Perhaps the clearest takeaway from Tuesday's US midterms is that data centers are unpopular. After a short-lived construction boom, they provide little ongoing employment and drive up local energy costs. There were 41 local votes on data center curbs and 40 of them are on track to win, with margins in the 75/25% range.

Microsoft and Amazon are heavily into the data center business, including huge plans to build more so they should be losers today, right? Wrong. Shares of those two are up around 7% and the market cheers a slower, smaller data center buildout. The market has been hating the massive spending on highly-inflated chips and data center supply chains.

In effect, the market is saying that the government is doing for you what you should be doing. Now the companies themselves have been trying to sell Wall Street on data center economics but the cash demands are simply too high and the market has said that the risk-reward isn't convincing. 

At this point, there might be some reflexivity in company management. Now that they've seen how the stock reacts to data center curbs, they might slow their own ambitions to levels closer to matching free cash flow. If so, that could be a powerful tailwind for the stocks, which have struggled this year.

Amazon is particularly compelling as its core business of goods delivery isn't under threat from AI in the same way as a software company like Microsoft. 

The flipside is that the companies in the data center building business are struggling. The neoclouds and vendors are all down big today, along with the companies that would be contract to provide the power to the data centers. 

Forthe next moves, watch what kind of agenda congressional Democrats set around AI and data centers. They have a wide menu of things to choose to go after, including rampant corruption. I tend to think that some level of oversight around AI is coming but I'm not sure they want to take on data centers at the national level. 

Another spot to watch is in Texas and Ohio, where more than one-quarter of planned data center capacity is located. Both of the new Democratic governors campaigned against data centers and it will be critical to see how they plan to act.

Most important those are voters, who have clearly showed they don't want to pay higher electricity rates so OpenAI can run the data centers harder.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Memory names getting smoked: Micron breaks the July low in 12% drop
item.description:
Shares of Micron have taken an ugly turn today, dropping 12% and breaking support at the July low.

Chip stocks are down heavily as the market re-thinks the pace of the AI build out. There are a few reasons for the change in thinking:

  1. The election showed US voters are heavily against data centers, with 40 of 41 direct votes on them failing and many candidates who were pro-data center losing
  2. The market initially rewarded the hyperscalers for those votes, showing that stock prices will improve if they slow spending
  3. Various reports show it will be impossible to power the pace of building data centers
  4. If data centers can be built, public opposition will result in higher costs because companies will have to pledge to build all the power infrastructure to go with them, essentially moving them off grid

The flip side of the argument is that Micron is making tremendous amounts of money right now and the order book is deep. The actual result for FY26 was $74.33 per shares, and that puts it at 9.3x this year's earnings. Moreover, the consensus rises to $177 for the fiscal year that just started so just 4x earnings. The consensus rises to $212 for 2028 but I wouldn't weigh that too heavily.

For what it's worth, the company has said the industry will be more supply-constrained in both 2027 and 2028 than in 2026. For HBM, they said a large portion of output is sold. Micron also said at the end of the quarter that more than 75% of production is committed.

Notably, Micron is trying to diminish its traditional cyclicality. It has signed 26 strategic customer agreements, expected to cover more than 35% of cumulative revenue through 2030. Approximately 75% of that revenue has defined pricing arrangements, primarily floors and ceilings. These agreements are multiyear take-or-pay contracts.

Despite that, there is some major variance in analyst revenue estimtes for the next two years.

The next thing to watch is the chart, it's ugly. Today's break of the July low cuts through support and puts it back at May levels.

Another data center buildout darling -- Caterpillar -- has already turned negative on the year after rising 86% YTD in late June. The market could be seeing technical changes coming from advanced models that need less memory, or this could be about the buildout.

Another possibility -- which I put a high weight on -- is that this is an irrational, emotional market. It's filled with fast-money options traders that trade on momentum. There is little thought given to earnings except on earnings data. After that, it's all an AI sentiment trade and right now there is an ebb in AI sentiment.

That said, I do think those earnings numbers are grounded in reality and it's hard to see a total cliff before 2029. That should make something like 3x next year's earnings akin to an absolute floor and that's around $530. There is also some support at $661, which was the mid-May low. 

Micron's next earnings report is likely to be in mid-to-late December.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil tests the key confluence area and finds willing buyers
item.description:
Crude oil futures fell sharply yesterday as traders weighed the chances of an end to the war with Iran. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats would push to end the war and pointed to support from some Republicans. Crude was down close to 8% when I wrote about the move.

The headlines helped drive the selloff. The technicals gave traders a place to lean against. Yesterday, I highlighted three levels within 27 cents of one another. The 50% midpoint of the move up from the July low came in at $86.93, the 100-day MA at $86.81 and the 200-day MA at $86.66. A move below that area that could stay below would give sellers room to roam. A hold would give buyers a shot at a bounce. Yesterday’s crude oil analysis

Today’s low reached $86.65, a penny below the 200-day MA, and bounced. Crude is trading at $89.26, up $1.17, or about 1.3%, after reaching a high of $90.35.

What do buyers need to get above?

After a sharp move like yesterday’s, I like to measure the last trend leg to see how much of it buyers can take back. On the 5-minute chart, measuring from yesterday’s high to today’s low puts the 38.2% retracement at $90.68. Today’s high of $90.35 fell 33 cents short. As long as the price stays below $90.68, the sellers still have the upper hand on that trend leg.

Get above $90.68 and stay above, and the focus shifts to $91.56, the broken 38.2% retracement of the broader rally from the early July low. Reclaiming that level would give buyers another reason to press toward $91.92, the 50% midpoint of the latest selloff. Taking back half of that decline would give buyers more control in the short term.

Where is the risk for buyers?

On a move lower, watch the 100- and 200-bar MAs on the 5-minute chart. A sustained move below both would tilt the short-term bias back toward the sellers and bring the $86.66–$86.93 support area back into focus. If sellers can get below today’s $86.65 low and stay below it, they’ll have done what they couldn’t do on the first test.

Trading lesson — How much of the selloff can buyers take back?

After a sharp selloff, I look for two clues. First, where do buyers show up? Second, how much of the decline can they take back? In crude oil, the first clue came at $86.65, where the price tested the 200-day MA and bounced. The second clue comes at $90.68, the 38.2% retracement of the last leg lower.

I use 38.2% as a minimum retracement when judging whether buyers are starting to take back control. If the bounce stalls below that level, sellers still have the advantage on that leg. If the price gets above it and holds, especially on a retest, buyers have a nearby level to lean against. That gives them a way to define their risk while looking for the next target.

There are two 38.2% levels in this setup because they measure two different moves. $90.68 measures how much of the latest selloff buyers have taken back. $91.56 measures the pullback of the broader rally from July and marks a level crude broke on the way down. Clearing the first would strengthen the bounce. Reclaiming the second would show buyers starting to repair some of the damage on the hourly chart.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Marco Rubio ‘on resignation watch’ - report
item.description:
The Independent reports that Marco Rubio "is on resignation watch from both sides of the Atlantic in the expectation he will quit to lauch a bid to be the next US President".

The report cites "senior party sources in the US and senior figures in the UK government" and notes that he was plotting his exit even before the disasterous midterms. 

Rival JD Vance already distanced himself from Trump by tring to take an anti-war stance and blaming the Iran war for the Republicans loss. It may be tough for him and Rubio to cast themselves as opponents to war after defending it in the first 9 months of fighting.

The Independent said up to five members of Trump's cabinet are considering runs for President. As for Rubio, a source said he needs “distance himself from the Iran war and pin that one on Trump.”

I had thought that Rubio would stick around as Secretary of State for a longer period because Cuba has been his longstanding issue and the US appers to be plotting regime change their. Rubio's family immigrated from Cuba prior to Fidel Castro's revolution.

In betting markets, the odds for Ron DeSantis have improved dramatically this week as he launches critcisms of the administration as an outsider.

This is the nature of politics and now that the Iran war is seen as a failure, none of them will want to take responsibility for it. Meanwhile, none of them resigned in February when the war started, so Vance and Rubio will be vulnerable to attacks from other candidates who say they were never the "America First" politicians they said they were.

At the same time, if any of them distance themselves too far from Trump, he will turn thin-skinned and sabotage their candidacies. That set-up may make it easier for outsiders to take leadership of the party.

However given the results of the primaries, the real battle to get a Republican president in the next election may come down to policymaking in the next two years. If tariffs, inflation and the Iran war are still going on in 2028, it's tough to imagine any of them having a real chance, given the results on Tuesday.

item.title: US Q3 productivity +3.6% vs +2.8% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +1.4%
  • Unit labor costs -0.7% vs +0.6% expected
  • Prior unit labor costs +1.2%

On the face of it, these look strong disinflationary but these numbers are largely ignored by policymakers because they're notoriously volatile and hard to measure.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its Productivity and Costs report quarterly. A preliminary estimate comes out roughly five weeks after the quarter ends, followed by a revised estimate about a month later that incorporates updated GDP and labor data.

The headline measure is labor productivity in the nonfarm business sector, defined as output per hour worked. It’s reported as an annualized quarterly rate and as a year-over-year change. Output is derived from GDP, excluding government, households, nonprofits and farms, while hours come from the BLS employment surveys. Productivity growth is the main long-run driver of living standards, because it determines how fast incomes can rise without generating inflation.

Unit labor costs measure what businesses pay in compensation to produce one unit of output. They’re calculated as hourly compensation divided by productivity. When wages rise faster than productivity, unit labor costs climb, which can squeeze profit margins or push companies to raise prices. That makes the measure a closely watched input in the inflation outlook and in the Federal Reserve’s assessment of whether wage growth is consistent with its 2% target.

The report also includes figures for manufacturing and for nonfinancial corporations, along with hourly compensation and real hourly compensation.

The quarterly numbers are noisy and prone to large revisions, particularly as GDP and compensation data are updated. For that reason, economists tend to focus on multi-quarter and annual trends. The report rarely moves markets, but productivity has drawn renewed attention as investors and policymakers look for signs that artificial intelligence is lifting output per worker and allowing faster growth without added inflation.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US initial jobless claims 189K vs 196K estimate
item.description:
• Prior week initial claims 194K
  • Prior week continuing claims 1.701M

Details

  • Initial jobless claims (October 31) fell 6,000 to 189,000. Prior revised to 195,000 from 194,000.

  • Initial claims four-week average fell 2,250 to 194,750. Prior revised to 197,000 from 196,750.

  • Continuing claims (October 24) rose 23,000 to 1,718,000. Prior revised to 1,695,000 from 1,701,000.

  • Continuing claims four-week average rose 1,000 to 1,709,500. Prior revised to 1,708,500 from 1,710,000.

  • Insured unemployment rate (October 24) held at 1.1%.

U.S. initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 in the week ending October 31, the Labor Department reported. The four-week average also fell, pointing to fewer new filings even after smoothing out some of the weekly noise.

Continuing claims moved the other way, rising to 1.718 million in the week ending October 24. The four-week average edged up by just 1,000, so the rise was more pronounced in the weekly figure than in the recent trend.

Quick analysis

The drop in initial claims points to limited layoff pressure. On its own, that gives the Fed less reason to hurry toward a rate cut and can lend some support to the dollar and short-term Treasury yields. The rise in continuing claims tempers that signal because it can point to people taking longer to find work. The next few readings will show whether that rise is becoming a trend.

What this report measures

Initial claims count new filings for unemployment benefits and give traders an early read on layoffs. Continuing claims track ongoing filings and are reported with an extra week’s lag. Both headline figures are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision, and traders watch their four-week averages to gauge the labor-market trend.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoE Governor Bailey says there is a case for another 25bps hike if war doesn't end
item.description:
Governor Bailey warned that another 25 bps rate increase could be justified if the conflict in Iran does not come to an end. Bailey stressed that the UK needs to limit the inflationary impact of the conflict, particularly given that domestic inflation pressures were already elevated before the energy shock.

However, he pushed back against suggestions that the BoE has acted too late, arguing that the latest decline in oil prices was encouraging but that policymakers cannot place too much weight on short-term developments without clear evidence of a genuine peace process.

He also refused to commit to a "two and done" outlook for interest rates, highlighting the uncertainty surrounding the conflict and noting that he hopes to have greater clarity on its outcome by December.

Bailey also addressed market pricing, noting that the upward shift in the interest rate curve partly reflects higher risk premia rather than expectations of further policy tightening, describing the current pricing as a reasonable reflection of energy-related risks. On the domestic economy, he pointed to stronger-than-expected business investment.

On the inflation outlook, Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden said the downward trend in services price inflation appeared to have slowed or stopped. Lombardelli, meanwhile, noted that consumer-facing businesses were reporting less pricing power than business-to-business companies. She added that public-sector wages did not represent a particular inflation risk and that the latest minimum wage increase was broadly in line with, or below, expectations.

Overall, the BoE is reluctant to adopt a stronger hawkish stance, so the December meeting will depend heavily on developments in the US-Iran conflict, energy prices and evidence of second-round inflation effects in the economic data. The British pound spiked on the surprise 9-0 vote split, but gave back most of the gains on underwhelming commentary.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Bank of England decision and minutes

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said today’s quarter-point hike to 4% was justified by inflation pressures already in the pipeline, even after the latest drop in oil prices. He said the hike does not necessarily mark the start of a series, but the case for another 25 basis points could be fairly strong if the US–Iran conflict remains unresolved. Further progress toward a resolution could reduce the need for additional hikes and allow inflation to peak somewhat below 5%. Bailey said the UK economy has been more resilient than expected, though the strength has been concentrated, with AI investment accounting for about a fifth of GDP growth. Private-sector wage growth is expected to change little in the coming months, while food and core goods inflation are likely to pick up. How long the conflict lasts and how energy costs feed through to broader inflation will help determine the BOE’s next move.

UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and the BOE expects it to approach 5% by mid-2027 as higher energy prices feed into household and business bills. Stronger-than-expected activity helped make the case for today’s hike. For the next decision, I’ll be watching whether those higher costs start showing up in wages and a wider range of prices. item.title: Bank of England raises the Bank Rate to 4.00% as expected in a 9-0 vote
item.description:
• Bank Rate at 4.00% as widely expected
  • Prior was 3.75%
  • Vote split 9-0 vs 7-2 expected
  • One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%
  • UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year
  • While the direct effects of higher energy prices are clear, and will continue to feed into firm and household energy bills, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages
  • Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, adding to the case for modestly tighter monetary policy
  • Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path
  • The Committee will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour, and slack
  • The Committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2% target in the medium term
  • Full statement

The Bank of England raised interest rates by 25 bps to 4.00% as widely expected, as policymakers become increasingly concerned about the inflationary consequences of the conflict in the Middle East. The decision was supported by an 8-1 majority, with one member voting for a larger 50 bps increase to 4.25%.

The BoE noted that UK CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September and is now expected to approach 5% by mid-2027, reflecting the continued rise in global energy prices. Although the direct impact on household and business energy bills is clear, the Committee stressed that there is still limited evidence of significant second-round effects on wages and other prices.

Nevertheless, policymakers judged that the inflationary pressures building in the pipeline were sufficient to warrant a rate increase. Stronger-than-expected economic activity data in recent months also added to the case for tighter monetary policy.

The BoE stressed that monetary policy is not on a pre-set path and that decisions will be made on a meeting-by-meeting basis. The Committee will pay particular attention to underlying wage growth, businesses' pricing behaviour and the degree of economic slack to assess whether higher energy costs are spreading into broader inflation. This suggests policymakers want to retain flexibility rather than commit to a prolonged tightening cycle.

However, the comments in the minutes showed a relatively hawkish debate within the MPC. Lombardelli and Pill see a case for further rate increases in the near term, with Pill suggesting that a single 25 bps hike is unlikely to be sufficient. Greene also indicated that additional increases will probably be required, while Mann warned that the economy is now operating in a more challenging environment for second-round inflation effects.

On the other side, Taylor and Dhingra viewed today's increase primarily as insurance against worse inflation outcomes. Governor Bailey added that part of the recent rise in market interest-rate expectations reflects higher risk premia rather than expectations of further policy tightening, arguing that current monetary conditions are broadly appropriate.

The BoE raised its 2027 GDP growth forecast to 1.3%, from 1.1% previously, while warning that economic activity is likely to weaken over the coming quarters. Unemployment is now expected to reach 5.1% in 2028, compared with 5.2% in the previous projections, while private-sector regular wage growth is forecast to remain relatively resilient, reaching 3.5% in Q4 2027.

Overall, today's decision signals that the BoE is increasingly concerned about the risk of energy-driven inflation becoming entrenched, but remains cautious given the limited second-round effects. Nevertheless, traders added to BoE rate hike bets and are now pricing a 50% chance of another increase in December.

item.title: What Could Stop the Fed Raising Rates in December?
item.description:
A December rate increase remains the market’s expected outcome. Investing.com’s rate  monitor put the probability of a quarter-percentage-point increase at about 80% on 4  November. Another hold would depart from that expectation, making the evidence that  might persuade the Federal Reserve to wait particularly relevant for traders. 

The Fed raised its benchmark rate to 3.75–4% in September and left it unchanged on 28  October. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan supported the hold, then argued two days later  for at least two more quarter-point increases. Her position illustrates how officials can  favour further tightening while allowing more time between decisions. 

A similar pause came in June 2023, when the Fed held rates to assess incoming information  and earlier tightening before raising them again in July. This time, the case for waiting  depends on whether inflation continues to ease and subdued hiring develops into broader  employment weakness. 

Inflation Has Eased Unevenly 

The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% between September  2025 and September 2026, above the Fed’s 2% annual inflation target. Prices excluding food  and energy, known as core inflation, increased 0.3% in both August and September 2026.

Across the third quarter of 2026, however, core inflation slowed to an annualised 2.5%, from  3.3% in the second quarter. These figures express each quarter’s price increases as an  annual rate. They show improvement over the broader period, while the latest monthly  readings leave its durability open to question. 

Energy prices add uncertainty. EBC analyst Edgar Peredo identifies disruption around the  Strait of Hormuz as a potential source of persistent inflation, as higher fuel costs feed into  transport and production. Oil nevertheless fell more than 8% on 4 November as investors  assessed prospects for Middle East peace following the US elections. 

Democrats won both chambers of Congress and will take control in January. The result  prompted investors to reassess the outlook for the conflict and future government spending,  although the legislative consequences remain ahead. Sustained lower oil prices would help  ease inflation pressure; renewed supply disruption would threaten that relief. 

October’s consumer inflation report, due on 10 November, will provide the next major  update on prices. Several softer readings would make a stronger case for patience than a  short-lived decline in oil alone. 

Slower Hiring Could Strengthen the Case for Waiting 

Payrolls increased by 29,000 in September 2026, while July and August’s combined gains  were revised down by 60,000. Unemployment edged up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August,  although it remained within the narrow range recorded since March. 

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offered a more reassuring assessment at his October press  conference, pointing to low unemployment insurance claims. The October jobs report,  scheduled for 6 November, will help establish whether September’s subdued hiring  continued. 

Further weak hiring alongside rising unemployment would increase the risk that higher  borrowing costs deepen a slowdown. Steadier employment would give officials more scope 

to respond to persistent inflation. The distinction is important for December: a resilient  labour market makes an increase easier to absorb, while the inflation outlook determines  whether further restraint is warranted. 

Borrowing Conditions Remain Uneven 

Warsh said financial and credit conditions had tightened for some households and  businesses since September’s increase. His assessment distinguished that recent  tightening from the overall level of borrowing conditions. The Fed’s October lending survey  provides a similarly mixed picture: standards tightened for small-business and commercial  property loans, while those for large and medium-sized business loans were broadly  unchanged. 

Business loan demand weakened partly because companies needed less financing for  investment and partly because they found more attractive funding elsewhere. Some  borrowers are reducing their investment needs, while others are changing lenders. Broader  evidence of declining investment and hiring would strengthen the argument for allowing  September’s increase more time to work. 

What Bond Yields Mean for the Dollar and Gold 

Peredo emphasises that gold’s response to weaker employment also depends on bond  yields, the dollar, and investor demand. Each can change for reasons beyond the next Fed  decision. 

The market moves on 4 November provide a recent example. Gold rose 2.2% by 06:19 GMT  as the dollar weakened and Treasury yields declined. Later that day, Reuters reported the  benchmark 10-year Treasury yield at 4.89%, down about six basis points. These were  readings from different points in the session, but both reports described support for bonds  as investors reassessed the outlook after the election.

Lower expected US interest rates generally weaken support for the dollar. For gold, falling  bond yields after allowing for expected inflation reduce the appeal of interest-paying  alternatives. Longer-term yields also reflect inflation and government borrowing  expectations, so their response can differ from changes in the probability of a December  increase. 

A hold would become more plausible if easing inflation were accompanied by broader  employment weakness. Whether that shift supported gold would also depend on the  response of bond yields and the dollar. Traders therefore have two related developments to  assess: the evidence shaping the Fed’s decision and the returns available elsewhere in  financial markets.

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq futures rebound nearly 280 points. But buyers now face a crucial test
item.description:
Nasdaq 100 futures | Technical analysis | November 5, 2026

The overnight recovery has survived renewed selling, with buyers defending higher prices and pushing Nasdaq futures back toward resistance. The next challenge is turning that rebound into a sustained move above 28,476.

Nasdaq 100 futures have staged an impressive overnight rebound, recovering nearly 280 points from their low of 28,167.75 to reach 28,447. But while the recovery shows encouraging signs beneath the surface, buyers have yet to prove that this is more than a temporary rebound within a broader correction.

The December 2026 Nasdaq 100 futures contract (NQ) was trading around 28,424 as of 05:37 EST (10:37 UTC) on November 5.

The most important question now is whether buyers can overcome resistance between 28,447 and 28,476, or whether sellers will use the recovery as another opportunity to regain control.

Why this Nasdaq rebound deserves attention

A market can rebound sharply simply because selling pressure temporarily subsides. That does not necessarily mean a lasting bullish reversal has begun.

What makes this particular recovery interesting is how Nasdaq futures behaved when sellers attempted to push prices lower again.

After reaching the overnight low near 28,168, futures recovered above 28,300. Then came an important test: prices retreated toward 28,274 but stopped well above their earlier low.

Buyers subsequently returned, pushing futures back above 28,400.

That sequence matters because the market did more than bounce. It established a higher low, defended it, and resumed its advance.

This suggests that sellers were becoming less effective at pushing prices lower, at least during the period examined.

There is another interesting detail.

Some advances occurred without particularly strong aggressive buying activity. In other words, prices managed to climb even though buyers were not consistently overwhelming sellers.

One possible interpretation is that selling pressure was losing effectiveness. Another is that available liquidity was relatively thin, allowing prices to move higher with less buying activity.

Neither interpretation proves that a lasting reversal is underway. But the combination of a defended higher low and renewed upward progress makes the recovery worth watching.

Nasdaq futures reclaimed an important average price

Another constructive development was the move back above the overnight volume-weighted average price (VWAP), near 28,352 at the analysis cutoff.

VWAP measures the average price paid over a specified period, with greater weight given to prices where more trading occurred.

For traders, it offers a useful way to assess whether the market is trading above or below an important reference price.

Recovering above that level suggests the short-term balance has improved for buyers.

However, the more important test is whether Nasdaq futures can remain above this area when sellers return.

A market that briefly reclaims an important level but immediately falls back below it has not demonstrated the same strength as one that successfully defends the recovery during a pullback.

That distinction is particularly relevant now, with resistance immediately overhead.

The critical resistance area: 28,447 to 28,476

The recovery reached 28,447 before pulling back modestly.

That places Nasdaq futures close to an important resistance region extending toward 28,476.

A move above this zone would be encouraging, but traders should distinguish between briefly trading above resistance and actually establishing support there.

For example, a breakout followed by a successful retest of the former resistance area would offer stronger evidence of bullish control than an isolated move above 28,476.

If buyers establish sustained trading above that level, the next potential recovery area lies between 28,500 and 28,545.

Conversely, another rejection near resistance could indicate that sellers remain active at higher prices.

The market has already demonstrated that buyers can defend a pullback. It has not yet demonstrated that they can overcome this overhead supply.

Nasdaq 100 futures: Key technical levels to watch

28,447-28,476 | Immediate resistance

The first major obstacle. Sustained trading above this region would strengthen the bullish recovery case.

28,500-28,545 | Next upside area

A potential destination for the recovery if buyers establish control above immediate resistance.

28,420-28,435 | Near-term battleground

An area where traders can assess whether the recovery is maintaining its immediate momentum.

28,350-28,370 | Important support

A key reference around the overnight VWAP and previously active trading region. Defending it would help preserve the recovery structure.

28,273-28,316 | Earlier defensive zone

The region associated with the recovery's higher-low structure. Sustained weakness below it would materially damage the short-term bullish case.

28,167.75 | Overnight low

The deeper reference for assessing whether the recovery has failed and the preceding decline is reasserting itself.

Three possible scenarios for Nasdaq futures traders

1. Bullish continuation: Buyers overcome resistance

The most constructive outcome would involve Nasdaq futures breaking above 28,476 and maintaining prices above that region.

A successful subsequent retest would further support the bullish interpretation.

Under those conditions, attention could shift toward 28,500-28,545.

However, traders should avoid treating every brief penetration of resistance as a confirmed breakout. The ability to maintain higher prices is what would provide the stronger evidence.

2. Consolidation: Buyers defend the recovery

Nasdaq futures could struggle near resistance without immediately turning bearish.

A pullback toward 28,350-28,370, followed by renewed buying, would suggest that the market is consolidating rather than surrendering its recent gains.

This would preserve the possibility of another attempt to challenge overhead resistance.

The distinction matters because a healthy recovery does not require prices to advance continuously. Pullbacks can help reveal whether buyers remain willing to support the market.

3. Bearish rejection: Sellers regain control

The warning signs would increase if Nasdaq futures repeatedly fail near 28,447-28,476 and subsequently fall below 28,350-28,370.

That combination would suggest that the recovery is losing momentum and that sellers are once again becoming more effective.

The next area to monitor would be 28,273-28,316.

Sustained trading below that defensive region would seriously undermine the short-term rebound, leaving the overnight low of 28,167.75 as the deeper reference.

Importantly, a retreat into support would not automatically confirm this bearish scenario. The market's reaction at those levels would matter.

The lesson for traders: A strong rebound is not necessarily a bullish reversal

One of the challenges in trading market reversals is recognizing the difference between the early signs of improving conditions and confirmation that a broader trend has changed.

Waiting for every possible confirmation can mean missing much of the initial recovery. Acting on the first bounce, however, carries the risk of entering a move that quickly fails.

The Nasdaq's overnight action illustrates that tension.

The recovery has already provided evidence that buyers can defend higher prices, even after renewed selling. That is constructive and should not be dismissed simply because the broader market structure remains uncertain.

But buyers still face another challenge: proving they can overcome resistance and defend the higher ground.

For now, 28,476 is the key upside test, while 28,350-28,370 is an important area for assessing whether the recovery remains intact.

The Nasdaq 100 futures rebound has passed its first meaningful test. Whether it becomes something more durable will depend on what happens next.

I'm also watching macro cross-currents and election fallout dominate positioning across the board today. In commodities, crude experienced a steep selloff while bullion ripped higher, creating a pivotal tape where gold jumped past $4,000 while oil slumped on Iran diplomacy hopes, putting Citi's thesis on diplomatic de-escalation driving precious metals directly to the test.

Across digital assets, sentiment has turned sharply constructive in the wake of the vote, but I need to see how order flow behaves around key liquidity overhead: Bitcoin bulls are back post-midterms, yet the $82,000 price magnet could change everything if price acceptance fails to hold above critical resistance.

At the same time, mounting fatigue over aggressive artificial intelligence capital expenditures has triggered a tangible sector rotation: while hyperscalers navigate shifting budget priorities, Berkshire added $27 million of Sirius XM as investors rotate from AI toward value stocks and cash-generative plays.

That pivot away from energy-intensive tech infrastructure is finding heavy fundamental backing in the political arena, where local ballot outcomes revealed that the biggest loser of the US elections was data centers amid stiff community opposition and tighter local regulatory hurdles.

Market analysis based on the December 2026 Nasdaq 100 futures contract as of November 5, 2026, 05:37 EST. All quoted prices and technical levels refer to that historical snapshot, not live market conditions. Futures trading involves leverage and substantial risk. Educational only. Trade at your own risk.
